one_liner: Squashes any number into a probability between zero and one.
everyday: Often a model produces a raw score that can be any number—huge, tiny, negative. But sometimes we need that score to be a probability: a number between zero and one that tells us how confident we are about something. The sigmoid takes any score and squashes it into that range.

The shape is a smooth S-curve that sits flat near zero on the left, rises steeply in the middle, and flattens near one on the right. Small changes in the score move the probability a lot when the score is close to zero, but have little effect when the score is very positive or very negative. This works by design because the flat parts (where the curve hardly moves) sit at the extremes—once the score is strongly positive or negative, the output probability is already nearly one or nearly zero, so adding more evidence barely budges it further.
symbols: the raw score from the model, can be any number
the exponential of the negative score, which is always positive
one plus that exponential, the denominator that forces the result between zero and one
the final output, the sigmoid function, always between zero and one
matters: Any binary decision in machine learning needs a probability: is this email spam, is this tumor malignant, does this image contain a cat. The model learns to output a raw confidence score, then the sigmoid converts it into a true probability between zero and one. This probability can then be compared against what actually happened (yes or no) to compute how wrong the model was, which drives learning.
